tip: 'On va au supermarché': on is spoken French for 'we', but the verb stays in the he/she form – on va, never on allons.
French is 'at the phone,' not on it: il est au téléphone. Au is à + le. The radio works the same way – à la radio.

english: I'm looking for the train station.
tip: Chercher already means 'look for' – the 'for' is inside it: 'cherche la gare', never chercher pour. Attendre (wait for) is the same.
In French, 'dans' is used for enclosed spaces: 'dans un bureau' (in an office). Use 'à' for cities and 'en' for countries.
In French, 'elles' is used for an all-female group. Even one male in the group changes it to 'ils'.
Réfléchir needs à for whatever you think about: 'réfléchis à la question' = think about the question.
English lets you drop 'that' – 'he says he's busy.' French never can: il dit qu'il est occupé. Que shortens to qu' before a vowel.

target: On fait les courses le samedi.
english: We do the shopping on Saturdays.
tip: On has a second life as impersonal 'one/they': 'On fait les courses' can mean we do the shopping, or people in general do. Context decides.

target: L'hôtel est près de la gare.
english: The hotel is near the station.
tip: 'L'' replaces 'le' or 'la' before words starting with a vowel or silent 'h': l'hôtel, l'école, l'ami.

target: Je bois du café le matin.
english: I drink coffee in the morning.
tip: 'Du' (de + le) is the masculine partitive article meaning 'some'. Use for uncountable nouns: du café, du lait, du pain.
'Détester' = to hate. With abstract nouns, French requires the article: 'il déteste le bruit' (he hates noise).

target: Excusez-moi, je cherche la gare centrale.
english: Excuse me, I'm looking for the central station.
tip: 'Excusez-moi' (formal) / 'excuse-moi' (informal). Hyphen links verb and pronoun in imperative.

target: Nous commençons le travail à neuf heures.
english: We start work at nine o'clock.
tip: For -er verbs ending in -cer (commencer), add a cedilla before -ons: nous commençons. This keeps the soft 'c' sound.

target: Est-ce que tu connais un bon restaurant ?
english: Do you know a good restaurant?
tip: 'Est-ce que' literally means 'is it that' – drop it in front of a statement and it turns into a yes/no question with no word-order change: 'Est-ce que tu connais...'.

target: Bonsoir, le dîner est servi dans le salon.
english: Good evening, dinner is served in the living room.
tip: Un salon is a living room, not a hair salon: le dîner est servi dans le salon means dinner's served in the lounge.
Nationality adjectives agree in gender: français/française, anglais/anglaise. They are not capitalized in French.
Adjectives with 'nous' and 'vous' forms of être must agree in number: 'nous sommes fatigués' (plural -s).
'Content' agrees in gender and number: content/contente/contents/contentes. The final -t is silent in masculine forms.
'Avoir chaud' = to be hot (personal feeling). Don't confuse with 'il fait chaud' (the weather is hot).
'Avoir raison' = to be right, 'avoir tort' = to be wrong. French says 'to have reason/wrong'.
Je suis désolé is literally 'I am devastated' – désoler means to distress or lay waste. French apologizes by claiming to be crushed.
Use 'être' for professions. In French, no article before the profession: Elle est médecin (not 'elle est une médecin').
Faire la fête is 'to party' – literally 'to make the party.' French reaches for faire where English uses 'have': ils font la fête.
Venir de + infinitive means 'just did', not 'come to': 'venons de finir' = we just finished. The de is what flips it to the recent past.
French can't say 'I think so' bare – it needs an object: je crois que oui is literally 'I believe that yes.' The 'que oui' is fixed.
Offrir looks like 'offer' but means to give as a gift: elle offre des fleurs = she gives flowers as a present, not merely offering them.
'Avoir soif' = to be thirsty. French uses 'to have thirst', not 'to be thirsty'.
'Être en retard' vs 'être en avance' (early). Both use 'en' before the noun.
No question word, no inversion – just lift your voice: tu es malade ? is a full question by intonation alone, marked only by the ?
'Aller' is used for health: 'Tu vas bien ?' = Are you doing well? Literally 'You go well?'
